newsitem.title: USA: Center tanks hot safety debate a year after TWA 800.
newsitem.headline: Center tanks hot safety debate a year after TWA 800.

text.p: The ultimate cause of the explosion that ripped apart TWA Flight 800 a year ago this week may remain a mystery, but the safety debate about centre fuel tanks is only going to heat up.

Safety officials and the airline industry are staking out positions on whether anything more should be done to prevent what has been a relatively rare event -- the explosion of fuel fumes resulting in total destruction of an aircraft.
Investigators are united in blaming the TWA crash that killed 230 people on the explosion of the centre fuel tank. But what touched it off is in doubt.

The National Transportation Safety Board has proposed a number of measures to minimise the chances of a similar blast but the Federal Aviation Administration and the airlines are not rushing to embrace them.

"I see it as more of the same from the FAA," said Mary Schiavo, the former inspector general for the Department of Transportation whose recent book, "Flying Blind, Flying Safe", detailed lapses at the agency.
"I think it's their (the NTSB's) job to often be at loggerheads with the FAA and fight for safety," Schiavo said.

Most previous fuel tank explosion incidents in commercial jet aircraft since the late 1950s have involved fuelling and maintenance errors or lightning. Design changes have been made to minimise these ignition sources.
But an explosion in 1990 of a Boeing 737 centre fuel tank while the plane taxied in the Philippines remains a mystery.
Early suspicions of a bomb or missile bringing down the TWA Boeing 747 off Long Island as it left New York for Paris last July 17 have faded but have not been entirely ruled out.

"All of our efforts to date have failed to uncover any credible evidence that the loss of Flight 800 was the result of a criminal act," Federal Bureau of Investigation official James Kallstrom told lawmakers last week.
Unless new information comes forward, the FBI will likely end its investigation in 60 to 90 days, he said.
That will leave the NTSB grappling with a range of theories including static electricity, chaffed wiring or even a high-speed particle from space.
Back in December, once it became clear the centre tank under the passenger deck and between the wings was the epicentre of the blast, the NTSB issued proposals.
These ranged from nitrogen inerting of the vapour in the centre fuel tank down to filling the tank with a small amount of cool fuel before flight.
The FAA has already indicated its scepticism, calling for industry comment on the proposals and seeking further study, to the annoyance of the NTSB.
Representative James Oberstar from Minnesota, the ranking Democrat on the House Transportation Committee, recently described the NTSB-FAA dispute as a "hissy fit" and called for cooperation.
That may be hard to achieve. The airline industry, which is still suspected of having wide influence at the FAA, has strong reservations about the NTSB measures.
An airline industry official who requested anonymity, told reporters last week that the traditional approach of eliminating ignition sources remained the correct approach.

Describing centre tank explosions as the rarest kind of accident, he said airlines flew 90 percent of the time with fuel fumes within the flammable range and no amount of cold fuel could practically overcome this.
Nitrogen inerting gear could introduce its own safety hazards, including suffocation, if it malfunctioned.
The Air Travelers Association, a new advocacy group for passengers, is also cautious about the use of nitrogen on cost and safety grounds.

"Obviously the nitrogen inerting would be effective but it would involve massive infrastructure changes around the world," association founder David Stempler told Reuters. "I'm not sure we want to be sitting on nitrogen tanks either."
Stempler urged the FAA to look first at keeping the fuel cool, particularly the NTSB proposal for more insulation between the centre tank and air-conditioning equipment.
"I don't think we should be cooking the fuel in the first place," he said.
